title: Property tax reform in England: a fresh look (John Muellbauer, INET Oxford Working Paper No. 2026-24, 11 September 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full PDF obtained directly. curl with a browser user-agent on the INET Oxford publication page returned HTTP 200 and the page's own <a> markup exposed a direct PDF link (oms-inet.files.svdcdn.com/production/files/Property_Tax_Reform_In_England_A_Fresh_Look_WP_Sep_2026.pdf), which also returned HTTP 200 on curl (894KB, 13 pages). Extracted full text with PyMuPDF (~30,000 characters, all 13 pages, including figure captions and the reference list). This is a complete, A-grade full-text fetch of the primary working paper — no access ladder steps beyond a direct browser-UA curl were needed.
verdict: NEW PAGE research/muellbauer-2026-property-tax-reform-england (Core tier — Muellbauer is Tier 1, this is a live, numbered UK policy proposal directly engaging the wiki's central 2026 UK storyline) AND ENRICH people/andy-burnham.md (the paper is very likely the technical elaboration of the Muellbauer-Treasury talks already noted there) AND ENRICH people/john-muellbauer.md (currently a stub; this is a third, distinct, dated Muellbauer proposal that should not be conflated with his 2023 'green LVT' or 2025 farmland-LVT proposals already on the page). Lower-priority optional touch to places/united-kingdom.md's 'Is Land Undertaxed' / '2026 LVT Moment' sections — a one-sentence cross-reference only, since the paper does not itself engage the land-undertaxed question.
claim_grade: A — full primary text read directly, every figure, quote, and mechanism below verified against the fetched PDF (grep-confirmed for the LVT/Mirrlees negative finding specifically). Not a summary of a summary.
what_he_actually_proposes: This is NOT a general council-tax revaluation or land-value-tax proposal. It is narrow and specific: a redesign of the government's own November 2025 Budget policy, the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS) — a new banded surcharge on homes valued above GBP2m, VOA-administered, due live 2028, public consultation concluded July 2026. Muellbauer calls the government's HVCTS design 'seriously flawed' because it 'retains the principle of price bands, and associated cliff-edges, and caps the amount of tax collected at the upper end.' His alternative, the Proportional High Value Council Tax Surcharge (PHVCTS): a straight-line proportional rate applied only to the VALUE ABOVE a GBP1.5m threshold (not a land-value base — this is whole-property value, land+structure) — 0.5%/year for primary homes, 1%/year (double) for second/foreign-owned homes. Worked examples direct from the text: a GBP2m primary home pays GBP2,500/year; GBP3m pays GBP7,500; GBP5m pays GBP17,500 (double for second homes). He pairs this with a cut to Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) above GBP1.5m, but insists the SDLT cut must be TAPERED (his formula: discount = 100*(P-1.5)/P up to a GBP4m property, capped at 62.5% above GBP4m) rather than a flat halving, to avoid a horizontal-equity cliff-edge exactly at the GBP1.5m threshold. Deferral is built in for cash-poor/pensioner owners: a non-means-tested deferral option at a higher 0.6% rate (vs the standard 0.5%) to compensate the exchequer for lost interest, or a 0.7% automatic/means-tested deferral variant.
the_numbers: Revenue: Muellbauer cites Michael Dent's (Property Tax Lab / PropertyData.co.uk 'PRISM' model) estimate of about GBP2.21bn/year from the PHVCTS (GBP2.01bn from the GBP2m+ segment on an estimated 159,000 homes averaging GBP3.61m, plus GBP0.2bn from the GBP1.5-2m segment on an estimated 172,000 homes averaging GBP1.71m) — 'raise significantly more revenue than Rachel Reeves' version of HVCTS.' Muellbauer argues, via a lengthy discussion of Dent's transactions-vs-stock stratification methodology (2,163 local-authority-by-Council-Tax-band cells, composition-controlled regression on 12 variables), that this figure is likely a small UNDERestimate because high-value transactions data undercounts the stock outside London (high SDLT rates depress recorded transaction volumes relative to true stock at the top end). Scope: the reform affects 'only about 1.3 percent of properties in England.' Growth case: reduced incentive for 'expensive improvements and extensions' (basement-digging, citing Burrows, Graham & Wilson 2022 on London elite basements) that currently compete for scarce construction-industry capacity with volume housebuilding; reduced incentive to keep expensive homes empty/under-occupied (citing Atkinson & Mingay 2024 on London 'ultra-prime' towers); and a reversal of the current incentive to merge flats into a single high-value home for a lower Council Tax band — worked example: a GBP5m single home currently pays GBP17,500 PHVCTS (GBP35,000 if a second home) versus three GBP1.75m flats paying just GBP1,250 each as primary residences.
does_he_engage_lvt_or_mirrlees: No. Grep of the full extracted text for 'land value', 'LVT', 'Mirrlees', and 'land tax' returns zero hits. This paper is a proportional PROPERTY tax (whole value, not land value alone) confined to the top ~1.3% of the market, paired with SDLT reform — not a land-value-tax proposal and not an engagement with the Mirrlees Review's recommendation for a commercial LVT (which the wiki's places/united-kingdom.md 'Is Land Undertaxed' section already covers via the Henry George Foundation essay). Muellbauer explicitly defers the FULLER reform — 'a future reform of Council Tax towards a fair, proportional tax, abandoning Britain's idiosyncratic and defective banding system' — to a forthcoming companion paper he cites as Muellbauer (2026b), 'Land, Housing and the British Economy,' Journal of the British Academy 14(3), forthcoming, which is NOT yet published and was not available to fetch. That forthcoming piece, not this one, is the more likely place he engages land value and Mirrlees directly — worth flagging for a future ingestion pass once it appears.
burnham_link: The paper opens and closes by explicitly framing the proposal as an agenda item for Burnham's government: 'Andy Burnham has signalled a major shift in the focus of policy towards reducing regional and generational inequality, improving housing affordability while boosting growth, an agenda a joint reform of the HVCTS, combined with a cut in Stamp Duty would advance.' And in closing: 'The new Prime Minister has promised change in a more egalitarian direction and needs to distinguish his policies from those of his predecessor. Few policy shifts could better symbolise this new direction than the reforms proposed here.' No indication the paper reflects an actual government decision — it reads as Muellbauer's own advocacy piece directed at the new government, consistent with the existing wiki note (people/andy-burnham.md, source 19, Inman/Guardian 11 Aug 2026) that Muellbauer has 'held talks with Treasury officials about applying a percentage levy to top-end home values once the Valuation Office finishes the project' — this WP, published a month after that Guardian piece, is very plausibly the technical elaboration of exactly that idea, though the paper itself does not state that the Treasury talks concern this specific PHVCTS design.
existing_wiki_coverage: people/andy-burnham.md already has extensive 2026 UK property-tax-reform coverage (Fairer Share's 0.48% PPT, Neidle/TPA's 1.28% pure-LVT modelling, PolicyEngine's 0.77% LVT microsimulation, the Inman/Guardian OBR figures and the one-line Muellbauer-Treasury-talks mention) but nothing on the specific HVCTS/mansion-tax redesign this paper proposes — genuinely new, complementary detail, not a duplicate. people/john-muellbauer.md is a stub citing a 2023 'green land value tax' INET WP and a vaguer 2025 'wealth-style surcharge on top Council Tax bands plus a land value tax on farmland' proposal (sourced to INET news coverage, not a primary paper) — this September 2026 WP is a THIRD, distinct, and much more concrete/numbered proposal (top-value-tier surcharge + SDLT taper, no farmland element) and should be added as its own dated item, not merged into the 2025 farmland-LVT description. places/united-kingdom.md's 'Is Land Undertaxed' section (Leunig/Burnham exchange, Mirrlees Review's ~4% commercial LVT recommendation) is thematically adjacent but this paper does not itself weigh in on that debate — at most a one-line 'see also' cross-reference is warranted, not integration into that section's argument. research/tpa-what-would-lvt-do.md and research/ahmadi-ghenis-uk-council-tax-lvt-microsimulation.md both model a FULL, universal LVT replacing council tax outright (at 0.77-1.46% rates); Muellbauer's PHVCTS is a different animal — top-slice-only, whole-property-value based, paired with SDLT rather than replacing council tax outright — and a T1 building out a UK LVT comparison page/table should keep these clearly distinguished rather than treating all four (Fairer Share, Neidle, PolicyEngine, Muellbauer) as variants of 'the same' land tax idea, since only two of the four (Neidle's pure-LVT scenario and PolicyEngine's) are actually land-value-based.
uncertainties: 1. The companion paper Muellbauer (2026b), 'Land, Housing and the British Economy' (Journal of the British Academy 14(3), forthcoming), is referenced repeatedly as where the fuller reform case is made — it was not available to fetch (forthcoming/unpublished) and should be tracked for a future pass, since it is more likely to engage LVT and Mirrlees directly than this paper does. 2. Muellbauer's own January 2026 Financial Times piece ('The problem with the mansion tax is that it's badly designed,' cited here as Muellbauer 2026a) was not independently fetched this session (likely paywalled); the WP paraphrases its argument, which is sufficient for what is asserted in the WP itself but a fuller FT read could add texture. 3. Michael Dent / Property Tax Lab / PRISM (propertytaxlab.org.uk) has no existing wiki page — the revenue and transactions-vs-stock methodology this paper leans on heavily is currently uncited anywhere else on the wiki; a T1 may want to assess whether Dent/Property Tax Lab warrants its own page given its apparent centrality to current UK property-tax-reform modelling. 4. I did not independently verify Dent's PRISM revenue methodology or figures against Property Tax Lab's own site — they are reported here only as Muellbauer cites them. 5. Whether the Muellbauer-Treasury talks reported by Inman (Guardian, 11 Aug 2026) specifically concern this PHVCTS design, versus a different top-end valuation project, is not stated in either source and should not be asserted as confirmed without further sourcing.

title: They Raised Your Housing Costs by Doing Nothing: The Economist They Erased (Eric Daniel Buesing, personal site, 28 August 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full page fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, Ghost-hosted personal blog, no paywall). Parsed to clean text (stripped HTML/scripts/styles); the full essay body plus all 18 footnotes and the bibliography were read in full. Full-text A-grade fetch of the essay as published; no secondary or partial source.
verdict: REJECT for the essay itself, confirming the default expectation for a Tier-2 personal-site essay. One lead worth flagging separately and NOT via Buesing: a specific 2026 USDA survey he cites (see below) is a genuine Tier-1 primary source the wiki does not currently carry, and could be independently verified and cited in its own right if a T1 judges it useful — but never attributed to or sourced through this blog post.
claim_grade: D — a self-published personal-site essay by a non-economist author (a self-help/'conspiracy-adjacent' writer whose other works include a self-published book on 'Emergent Holopanentheism,' a spiritual cosmology framework, and a TrineDay-published book, 'The Hidden Hand: Wealth, Power, and Control from Pharaohs to Corporations,' 2026, that this essay is explicitly promoting). Under EDITORIAL Sec.4c this is squarely Tier 2 (blogger/practitioner-author; may be cited only as the origin/proponent of a claim, not as support), and under the source-quality hierarchy it sits at tier 6-7 (advocacy/blog, navigation only).
content_summary: A general-audience popular explainer of Henry George and economic rent, framed around a vacant-lot thought experiment and structured around the author's own narrative of having Henry George's ideas introduced to him by Marty Rowland (trustee/lecturer, Henry George School of Social Science) while writing the foreword to Buesing's own book. Restates standard George biography (1839-1897, Progress and Poverty 1879, 1886 NYC mayoral run against Theodore Roosevelt) with citations to Wikipedia-tier tertiary sources (Britannica Money, Encyclopedia.com) and O'Donnell's 2015 biography. Adds an extended argument, presented as speculative and explicitly hedged ('I can't point to a memo... I'd rather underclaim than overclaim'), that George's academic marginalization after his death fits a 'documented pattern' of land-speculation-funded universities and foundations shaping which economic questions got taken seriously — this is argued, not sourced to any specific study of the mechanism, and the essay itself flags it as circumstantial. A substantial middle section (roughly a third of the essay, footnotes 7-12) is a general history of colonial land dispossession (Virginia Company, Dutch West India Company, French/Swedish chartered companies, Mexican-era California ranchos culminating in Tejon Ranch, and 19th-century railroad land grants culminating in Catellus/New Nevada Lands) presented as background George 'gave little attention to.' The final third pivots to the author's own 'Emergent Holopanentheism' spiritual framework (a self-published 2025 work) as a theological grounding for treating land value capture as a moral obligation, then closes with a contemporary-relevance section on farmland concentration.
the_one_verifiable_specific: In the closing section, Buesing cites a real, checkable primary source: 'The USDA's most recent survey of farmland, released in March 2026, found that nearly 80 percent of all rented farmland is owned by landlords who don't farm it themselves... The survey also projects that over the next five years, owners plan to pass roughly 168 million acres to the next generation through wills and trusts rather than selling it on the open market. The average non-farming landlord is around 69 years old. More than a third are 75 or older, and that older group alone controls over 40 percent of the rental income and land value tied to it.' His footnote 17 cites this as: U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service, 2024 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL) Survey, released 12 March 2026 (nass.usda.gov), corroborated by a Farm and Dairy trade-press summary. This is a genuine, named, dated Tier-1 government survey — but the essay's own figures are Buesing's secondhand paraphrase, not independently verified against the primary NASS release in this session, and per Sec.4c a Tier-2 blogger cannot be the wiki's citation for it regardless.
existing_wiki_coverage: A repo-wide search found no existing wiki page citing the USDA TOTAL survey, 'non-operator landlord,' or 'rented farmland' ownership-concentration statistics — this specific data point (inheritance-driven, aging, absentee farmland ownership) is not currently on the wiki anywhere, making it a genuinely new fact IF and only if fetched and verified from NASS directly. No existing wiki page covers Eric Buesing, 'The Hidden Hand,' or 'Emergent Holopanentheism.'
uncertainties: 1. I did not independently fetch or verify the USDA NASS 2024 TOTAL Survey (nass.usda.gov) in this session — the 80%/168 million acres/69-years-old/40%-of-rental-income figures above are Buesing's paraphrase only and must be re-verified against the primary NASS release before any use. 2. The 'George was academically erased by land-speculation-funded universities' claim, though honestly hedged by the author himself, has no citation to a specific historiographical study in this essay and should not be used even as a Tier-2-attributed claim without a better source — it reads as informed speculation, explicitly labeled as such by its own author. 3. I have not assessed whether Marty Rowland or the Henry George School's 'Reality Economics' blog (cited as the venue for a Buesing Q&A) already have wiki coverage or warrant any; this was out of scope for the brief. 4. The essay's core George explainer content is entirely standard and already far better covered, with primary sourcing, on the wiki's existing George/Progress and Poverty pages — none of it is a plausible enrichment target even setting aside the Tier-2 problem.

title: Ricardo's Law: The Book That Explains Why Britain Keeps Failing (Peter Smith, 'Renegade Ecologist' / 'Peter Smith Rewilding' Substack, cross-posted to Blogspot, 5 September 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full page fetched directly via curl with a browser user-agent (HTTP 200, Blogspot-hosted, Substack-syndicated content, no paywall). Parsed to clean text; the full essay, its embedded pull-quotes, and the blog's sidebar/about content were all read. Full-text A-grade fetch of the essay as published.
verdict: REJECT, confirming the default expectation for a Tier-2 blog covering a Tier-2 book the wiki already holds at Heavy scan depth (books/harrison-ricardos-law.md). The essay adds framing (a Burnham-premiership news hook and an interview format with Fred Harrison) but no new fact about the book or its reception that clears the bar for citation; several figures it restates duplicate the wiki's existing primary-text-verified content, sourced better, elsewhere.
claim_grade: D — a personal Substack/blog essay by Peter Smith, described on his own site as CEO of the Wildwood Trust (a wildlife conservation charity) and a rewilding advocate, not an economist or Harrison-book scholar; framed explicitly as promotional ('Get your copy here' with a bookseller link) and structured as a paraphrased conversation with Harrison rather than independent analysis. Squarely Tier 2 under Sec.4c (practitioner/advocate/blogger) — citable only as the origin of a claim Smith himself makes, never as support for a claim about the book's content, since page-level verification of what the book actually says must come from the primary text (which the wiki already holds at Heavy scan depth).
content_summary: An essay/interview piece in which Smith recounts asking Fred Harrison, in a recorded conversation, which of his books to recommend; Harrison names 'Ricardo's Law' (2006) and calls it 'a manual for politicians.' The piece then walks through Ricardo's law of rent, Harrison's application of it to a London-to-North-East land-price gradient (including a claimed Domesday Book replication of the same 11th-century pattern), the book's 'tax clawback scam' thesis with a poorest-fifth/richest-fifth tax-burden comparison (38% vs ~35%, close to but not identical to the wiki page's already-sourced 37.9%/35.1% ONS 2002-03 figures), the Don Riley/Jubilee Line anecdote, a 'The Economics of Life and Death' chapter on regional mortality gradients (Blackpool vs London life expectancy), a boom-bust/property-cycle section citing a 700% house-price/1,700% land-price rise in Britain 1979-2005 and an Australian real-estate-downturn GDP-loss estimate, and closes by tying the book's argument to Andy Burnham's premiership and the government's new mansion tax/council-tax-band debate.
duplication_with_existing_wiki_content: Every substantive thread in this essay already has better-sourced wiki coverage: (1) books/harrison-ricardos-law.md itself is a Heavy-scan-depth page verified directly against the 2006 primary text (474pp, ISBN confirmed), covering the same tax-clawback thesis, the same free-rider-homeowner worked example, and a near-identical ONS tax-burden comparison (37.9%/35.1%, not this essay's rounded 38%/35%) with exact page citations (pp.40-44) that this blog essay lacks entirely. (2) The Don Riley/Jubilee Line anecdote already has its own dedicated, presumably primary-sourced wiki page, research/riley-taken-for-a-ride.md, plus coverage on places/london.md, concepts/land-value-capture.md, and concepts/law-of-absorption.md. (3) The 'Economics of Life and Death' mortality-gradient material is already covered via books/harrison-ricardos-law.md's own See Also link to 'Miller: Dying for Justice' (books/harrison-ricardos-law.md cites it for the ~50,000-premature-deaths/year England-and-Wales figure), a dedicated epidemiological source Harrison himself cites, which is a stronger anchor than this blog's secondhand paraphrase. (4) The Andy Burnham/premiership framing duplicates extensive, far more detailed and better-dated coverage already on people/andy-burnham.md.
anything_new_or_uncertain: Two details in this essay are NOT verified as already on the wiki's book page and could, in principle, be worth a future direct-primary-source check by a T1 deepening the book page itself (never sourced to this blog): (a) the specific 700% house-price / 1,700% land-price growth figures for Britain 1979-2005, and (b) the Domesday Book land-price-gradient replication claim. Both are presented by Smith without page citations and are one hop removed from the primary text (his own paraphrase of a conversation with Harrison, not a direct quotation of the book), so they do not meet the wiki's citation bar as presented here — flagged only as a possible lead for someone re-reading the primary text directly, not as content to add from this source.
existing_wiki_coverage: books/harrison-ricardos-law.md (Heavy scan depth, verified against primary text, last_reviewed 2026-07-05); research/riley-taken-for-a-ride.md; the wiki's existing Miller 'Dying for Justice' citation via the book page's See Also. No existing wiki page covers Peter Smith, 'Renegade Ecologist,' or Wildwood Trust, and none is warranted on the strength of this piece.
uncertainties: 1. I did not independently verify the 700%/1,700% 1979-2005 price-growth figures or the Domesday Book claim against Harrison's primary text (the wiki's existing book-page scan focused on the chapters and page ranges already cited there; these specific figures were not confirmed present or page-cited during this session). 2. The Harrison quote 'rent is the price we pay to participate as paid-up members of civilisation,' attributed by Smith to Harrison, is unverified against the primary book text or any other primary Harrison source in this session — it may be from the book, from the recorded conversation Smith describes, or from elsewhere in Harrison's writing; it should not be added to the wiki without locating its actual source. 3. Smith's own long-running blog (visible in its 'Popular posts' sidebar, dating to 2013) suggests he is a minor but long-standing UK LVT/rewilding advocate; I did not assess whether he individually warrants any wiki mention as a proponent, which was out of scope for this brief.
